audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Mathematics degree is taught in Dutch, with some courses in English. It builds from calculus, linear algebra, probability and proof to advanced analysis, algebra, topology and mathematical modelling. Students finish with a supervised research project, a thesis and seminar presentations.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Both UCR options develop calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods and probability. One applies these methods to algorithms and statistical models. The other uses them to study Earth systems and environmental data. Leiden offers a deeper sequence in proof and pure mathematics and requires a mathematics research project.

curriculum.routeLabel: Mathematics with an example set of mathematics electives
curriculum.limitation: This 180 EC example includes 6 EC of open choice in year one, 12 EC of mathematics electives in each of years two and three, and 30 EC of open study in year three.

componentNotes.math-4082alg2xy: One of the year-two mathematics electives shown here. It prepares students for Algebraic Curves.
componentNotes.math-4082dsbkxy: One of the year-two mathematics electives shown here. Combinatorics and Optimisation is required first.
componentNotes.math-4082algcvy: One of the year-three mathematics electives shown here. It requires Algebra 2 or equivalent preparation.
componentNotes.math-4082apimsy: One of the year-three mathematics electives shown here. It assumes introductory probability, statistics and programming.
componentNotes.math-4082bsd18y: The 18 EC includes the supervised project, thesis and two seminar presentations. Entry requires Seminar Presentation and Communication and at least 30 EC of mathematics at year two or above.

notes.text: The UCR plans share several mathematical and computational methods with Leiden. Leiden develops proof across successive courses in analysis and algebra, teaches topology and measure theory, and requires a supervised mathematics project.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
